network.overall_strategy: The network is organized around the two best-supported abiotic alanine hubs in the supplied literature: (i) hydrothermal access to pyruvate followed by reductive amination, and (ii) surface generation of HCN plus acetaldehyde followed by Strecker chemistry and aminonitrile hydrolysis. All experimentally mature abiotic routes are treated as converging first on a prebiotic alanine pool that is overwhelmingly DL or only weakly enantioenriched. Because the literature does not support a generally compelling direct route from simple achiral feedstocks to substantial L-alanine excess, the target is reached only after a separate, explicitly speculative postsynthetic L-enrichment step.

reactions.name: Ni3Fe-catalyzed CO2/H2 fixation to pyruvate

conditions.other: alkaline to near-neutral serpentinization-like fluids; hydrothermal mixing zone

reactions.mechanism: surface reduction of CO2 to adsorbed C1 species followed by C-C coupling to a C3 alpha-keto acid
reactions.reasoning: Beyazay et al. (2023) experimentally obtained formate, acetate and pyruvate from CO2/H2 over Ni3Fe, so CO2/H2 to pyruvate is established. This is the strongest upstream hydrothermal entry into the pyruvate hub in the supplied literature, but the same work also shows a major integration gap because the reported pyruvate concentration was only about 0.02 mM, far below many downstream alanine experiments.

reactions.name: Fe-S/CO hydrothermal carbonylation to pyruvate

conditions.other: subseafloor carbonyl-rich hydrothermal system; net stoichiometry summarizes a multi-step carbonyl chemistry

reactions.mechanism: CO-derived fragments undergo metal-sulfide-mediated carbonyl insertion and C-C coupling to a C3 alpha-keto acid
reactions.reasoning: Cody et al. (2000) reported pyruvate formation in high-temperature, high-pressure Fe-S/CO chemistry. This edge encodes that chemistry as a net CO/H2 carbonylation-reduction step rather than as a single elementary reaction, so it is more schematic and lower-confidence than rxn_001, but it captures an experimentally supported hydrothermal route into the same pyruvate hub.

reactions.name: Ni-catalyzed H2 reductive amination of pyruvate
agents: Ni metal or awaruite-like Ni surface
reactions.mechanism: ammonia condenses with pyruvate to an imine or iminium, then surface-activated H2 reduces the C=N bond
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) showed that Ni catalyzes H2-driven reductive amination of pyruvate with millimolar ammonium under mild aqueous conditions, and Kelley et al. (2005) provides a natural H2-rich alkaline serpentinization analogue. This is one of the strongest current routes from a metabolism-like intermediate to abiotic alanine, but it does not intrinsically select L over D.

reactions.name: Fresh Fe(OH)2-promoted reductive amination of pyruvate

conditions.other: anaerobic batch conditions; pH 8.8-9.5; two Fe(OH)2 inputs and two FeOOH outputs are implied by balance

reactions.mechanism: pyruvate first forms an imine or iminium with ammonia, then Fe(II) hydroxide supplies reducing equivalents while being oxidized to ferric oxyhydroxide
reactions.reasoning: Huber and Wachtershauser (2003) demonstrated efficient alanine formation from pyruvate with freshly precipitated FeS or Fe(OH)2. Here the Fe(OH)2 variant is chosen because it allows explicit redox bookkeeping in the network; ferric oxyhydroxide is used as a chemically reasonable oxidized Fe sink. Their mineral should be treated as a stoichiometric redox-active promoter rather than a trace catalyst. Keefe et al. (1995) criticized broader CO2 plus FeS plus H2S autotrophic claims, but that critique does not remove the downstream pyruvate-to-alanine chemistry once pyruvate is present.

reactions.name: Mixed-valence iron oxyhydroxide-mediated amination of pyruvate

conditions.other: alkaline pH 9-10; sediment-like residence times; Fe(OH)2 here denotes the Fe(II)-rich component of the mixed precipitate

reactions.mechanism: iminium formation from pyruvate and ammonia is followed by electron transfer from Fe(II) sites within a partially oxidized iron precipitate, favoring amination over competing sinks
reactions.reasoning: Barge et al. (2019) found the highest alanine fractions with partially oxidized Fe(II)/Fe(III) oxyhydroxides at alkaline pH and warm temperature. This edge writes the Fe(II) component of that mixed solid as Fe(OH)2 oxidized to ferric oxyhydroxide, which captures the required redox asymmetry without treating the mineral as a simple spectator catalyst. The same study also showed that flow-through chimney analogues failed to make alanine, so this route is best supported for batch-like sediments or long-residence microenvironments rather than open vent chimneys.

reactions.name: Ni-rich meteoritic alloy-catalyzed H2 reductive amination of pyruvate

conditions.other: near-neutral to mildly alkaline aqueous system; exogenous metal surface

reactions.mechanism: heterogeneous H2 activation on Fe/Ni metal reduces the pyruvate-derived imine or iminium to alanine
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) also showed that Ni-bearing meteoritic Fe/Ni alloys catalyze H2-driven alanine formation from pyruvate and ammonium. This provides a distinct exogenous-catalyst variant of the same imine-reduction chemistry, but the environmental caveats are episodic meteoritic supply and the unusually high reactive surface area of powdered laboratory samples. Competing lactate formation remains significant.

reactions.name: Spark-discharge generation of HCN from methane and ammonia

conditions.other: local reducing plume; condensed water may be nearby even though not explicit in the net stoichiometry

reactions.mechanism: energetic discharge fragments reduced gases and recombines radicals to HCN while liberating H2
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1955, 1957) identified HCN as a primary discharge product from reduced gases, and later reanalyses of volcanic and H2S-containing experiments confirmed rich amino-acid precursor inventories (Johnson et al., 2008; Parker et al., 2011). This edge is a net representation of plasma chemistry rather than a one-step elementary process. Trail et al. (2011) weakens a globally persistent CH4/NH3 atmosphere, so the best environmental reading is local or transient reduced plumes rather than a permanently reducing whole atmosphere.

reactions.name: Spark-discharge generation of acetaldehyde from methane and water

conditions.other: water-rich discharge with condensation; net stoichiometry summarizes radical chemistry

reactions.mechanism: methane-derived carbon radicals are partially oxidized by water-derived oxygen and coupled to an aldehyde reservoir
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1957) argued that aldehydes are primary discharge products and key Strecker precursors, while volcanic-discharge variants broadened the accessible organic inventory (Johnson et al., 2008; Parker et al., 2011). The stoichiometry here is a net summary of complex plasma chemistry converting methane and water into acetaldehyde plus H2.

reactions.name: NiS-catalyzed acetylene hydration to acetaldehyde

conditions.other: alkaline hydrothermal fluid; CO was often co-present experimentally but is not required in the minimal balanced net step

reactions.mechanism: NiS activates acetylene toward hydration, likely via a vinyl intermediate that tautomerizes to acetaldehyde
reactions.reasoning: The 2023 Communications Chemistry acetylene-NiS study directly detected millimolar acetaldehyde from acetylene in water at 105 C and connected that chemistry to alanine formation after adding cyanide and ammonium. FeS alone did not give detectable free acetaldehyde, so NiS is chemically justified here. CO was present in the experiments and likely shaped surface chemistry, but the minimal balanced carbon transformation to acetaldehyde is hydration of acetylene. The same study showed that overall alanine yield remained low and depended strongly on pH and timing.

reactions.name: Classical Strecker formation of alaninonitrile

conditions.other: cyanide-rich aqueous solution; near-neutral to mildly basic conditions favor the amino-nitrile branch over lactonitrile accumulation

reactions.mechanism: acetaldehyde and ammonia form an amino alcohol and then an imine or iminium, followed by cyanide addition to give the alpha-aminonitrile
reactions.reasoning: For alanine, acetaldehyde plus NH3 plus HCN to alaninonitrile is the classical Strecker hub (Miller, 1957). Patel et al. (2015) independently support access to alanine aminonitrile precursors within a broader cyanosulfidic network. The main caveat is selectivity: acidic conditions divert acetaldehyde toward lactonitrile and lactic-acid chemistry rather than the aminonitrile branch.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of alaninonitrile to the prebiotic alanine pool

conditions.other: prolonged aqueous residence or wet-dry cycling; two water equivalents are implied by elemental balance

reactions.mechanism: the nitrile hydrolyzes stepwise through amide-like intermediates to the carboxylic acid, releasing ammonia
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1957) measured aminonitrile hydrolysis rates sufficient to account for amino-acid buildup in discharge experiments, making hydrolysis of alaninonitrile to alanine a well-supported terminal step. Because the upstream reagents are achiral, the product here is represented as a prebiotic alanine pool that is predominantly DL or only weakly enantioenriched, not as direct L-alanine.

reactions.name: Postsynthetic enrichment of L-alanine from a prebiotic alanine pool

conditions.other: iterated adsorption/desorption or dissolution/crystallization under wet-dry or thermal cycling; separation edge rather than de novo synthesis

reactions.mechanism: partial enantioenrichment of an initially near-racemic alanine pool by selective adsorption, crystallization, or related amplification at mineral interfaces
reactions.reasoning: This is explicitly the weakest and most speculative edge. Parker et al. (2011) found discharge alanine to be racemic within error, Bernstein et al. (2002) obtained racemic amino acids from ice photochemistry, and Li et al. (2024) showed that mineral-induced asymmetry can occur but favored D-alanine on natural pyrite rather than L-alanine. The edge is therefore included only because the requested target is L-alanine; it represents postsynthetic enrichment or separation from a pre-existing alanine pool, not a generally demonstrated direct abiotic synthesis of L-alanine.

pathways.name: CO2/H2 fixation plus Ni/H2 amination
pathways.description: Hydrothermal CO2/H2 fixation over Ni3Fe generates pyruvate, which is converted to the alanine pool by Ni-catalyzed H2 reductive amination. The target is reached only after the shared speculative L-enrichment step.

pathways.name: CO2/H2 fixation plus fresh Fe(OH)2 amination
pathways.description: CO2/H2 first feeds the pyruvate hub, then freshly precipitated Fe(OH)2 acts as a stoichiometric redox-active promoter for pyruvate amination. The last step remains speculative L-enrichment from the alanine pool.

pathways.name: CO2/H2 fixation plus mixed-iron oxyhydroxide amination
pathways.description: Ni3Fe-derived pyruvate is converted to alanine in an alkaline mixed Fe(II)/Fe(III) oxyhydroxide setting, a batch-like hydrothermal analogue of the Barge system. L-alanine still requires the common enrichment edge.

pathways.name: CO2/H2 fixation plus meteoritic Fe/Ni amination
pathways.description: Hydrothermally generated pyruvate is aminated by H2 on a Ni-rich Fe/Ni meteoritic alloy surface. This route is chemically supported but depends on exogenous catalyst supply and still reaches the target only via postsynthetic L-enrichment.

pathways.name: CO carbonylation plus Ni/H2 amination
pathways.description: A more schematic CO-rich hydrothermal route supplies pyruvate, which then undergoes Ni-catalyzed H2 reductive amination. This is lower confidence than P1 because the pyruvate-forming edge is a net representation of a more complex Fe-S/CO chemistry.

pathways.name: CO carbonylation plus fresh Fe(OH)2 amination
pathways.description: CO-derived hydrothermal pyruvate is converted to the alanine pool by freshly precipitated Fe(OH)2. As elsewhere, the experimentally grounded chemistry stops at a non-L-specific alanine pool and requires a separate enrichment step.

pathways.name: CO carbonylation plus mixed-iron oxyhydroxide amination
pathways.description: CO-based hydrothermal pyruvate formation feeds the mixed-valence iron oxyhydroxide alanine route. This combines a less direct upstream pyruvate source with one of the strongest downstream batch alanine-forming systems.

pathways.name: CO carbonylation plus meteoritic Fe/Ni amination
pathways.description: CO-derived pyruvate is reduced and aminated on a Ni-rich meteoritic alloy under H2. The chemistry is plausible in outline but inherits the lower-confidence schematic CO-to-pyruvate step and still needs the shared L-enrichment edge.

pathways.name: All-surface discharge Strecker route
pathways.description: Local reduced discharge chemistry supplies both HCN and acetaldehyde from methane-based feedstocks; classical Strecker formation of alaninonitrile followed by hydrolysis gives the alanine pool. This is chemically one of the best-supported abiotic routes, but only to a non-L-specific alanine pool.

pathways.name: Discharge HCN plus NiS-acetylene Strecker route
pathways.description: HCN is supplied by surface discharge chemistry, while acetaldehyde is supplied by NiS-catalyzed hydrothermal acetylene hydration; their convergence in aqueous Strecker chemistry gives alaninonitrile and then the alanine pool. This mixed-source path is experimentally grounded but low-yield and requires transport plus pH sequencing.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Good hydrothermal logic to a prebiotic alanine pool: CO2/H2 to pyruvate is experimentally established and Ni/H2 reductive amination of pyruvate is well supported. The main weaknesses are the very low demonstrated upstream pyruvate titre relative to downstream alanine studies and the unsupported postsynthetic L-enrichment step.
suggestions: Add an explicit pyruvate concentration, adsorption, or accumulation step between rxn_001 and rxn_003.
Replace rxn_012 with a concrete literature-backed chiral enrichment mechanism or redefine the target as DL or near-racemic alanine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Fresh Fe(OH)2-promoted amination of pyruvate is literature-supported, and treating Fe(OH)2 as a consumed redox-active promoter is appropriate. The route still inherits the low upstream pyruvate supply problem and does not provide a chemically specified path from the racemic alanine pool to L-alanine.
suggestions: Specify fresh precipitate, alkaline pH, and stoichiometric Fe(OH)2 loadings for rxn_004.
Replace rxn_012 with a defined enrichment mechanism or stop the pathway at the prebiotic alanine pool.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The mixed-iron batch chemistry is real, but rxn_005 is not a faithful encoding of the cited system. The literature support is for partially oxidized Fe(II)/Fe(III) oxyhydroxides under alkaline, warm batch conditions, not simply Fe(OH)2 being converted to FeOOH; the published chimney-flow analogue also did not give alanine.
suggestions: Recast rxn_005 to start from a mixed Fe(II)/Fe(III) oxyhydroxide phase rather than pure Fe(OH)2.
State the alkaline batch conditions and the negative chimney-flow result so the environmental scope is not overstated.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ni-rich meteoritic alloy plus H2 can reductively aminate pyruvate, so the downstream chemistry is credible. The weaker points are the same low-yield pyruvate supply issue as P1, the need to justify meteoritic metal availability and reactive surface area in the stated hydrothermal setting, and the unsupported L-enrichment step.
suggestions: Justify meteoritic alloy delivery, persistence, and accessible surface area in the hydrothermal environment.
Add an explicit pyruvate accumulation step and a real chiral enrichment mechanism.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: CO-based hydrothermal access to pyruvate is literature-grounded, but rxn_002 is encoded too coarsely relative to the cited Fe-S/high-temperature chemistry. Downstream Ni/H2 amination is strong, but the pathway still lacks a convincing integration between pyruvate formation and amination and has no supported route to L-alanine.
suggestions: Encode rxn_002 with the specific Fe-S and high-temperature context used in the literature, rather than as a generic CO plus H2 step.
Add a concentration or transfer step linking pyruvate generation to reductive amination.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This route is chemically plausible to a prebiotic alanine pool, but both the upstream CO-carbonylation step and the downstream Fe(OH)2-promoted amination need more explicit condition control than the current encoding provides. The final L-enrichment step remains entirely speculative.
suggestions: Specify the high-temperature Fe-S context for rxn_002 and the fresh Fe(OH)2, alkaline conditions for rxn_004.
Replace rxn_012 with a supported chiral selection step or end the pathway at DL or near-racemic alanine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the weakest hydrothermal pyruvate-family path as encoded, because both the CO-to-pyruvate step and the mixed-valence iron step are underspecified relative to the cited experiments. As written it is better supported as a rough route to an alanine pool than as a coherent, environment-specific synthesis of L-alanine.
suggestions: Rewrite rxn_005 to reflect mixed Fe(II)/Fe(III) oxyhydroxides rather than Fe(OH)2 alone.
Add the missing environmental details that link the CO-carbonylation chemistry to the alkaline batch amination chemistry.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Meteorite/H2 amination is experimentally supported, but combining it with the simplified CO-carbonylation upstream step creates two integration burdens at once. The pathway also needs a better justification for catalyst availability and still does not provide a defensible chemical route from a racemate to L-alanine.
suggestions: Justify both the CO-carbonylation conditions and the meteoritic-metal catalyst source in the stated setting.
Add an explicit mechanism for L-enrichment or stop at the racemic alanine node.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the best-supported end-to-end abiotic alanine route in the network. Discharge production of HCN and aldehydes, Strecker alaninonitrile formation, and aminonitrile hydrolysis all align well with classic Miller-style literature; the main caveats are contested bulk atmospheric redox, the need to manage NH3, HCN, and pH to suppress lactonitrile chemistry, and the unsupported L-enrichment step.
suggestions: State explicitly that the discharge setting is local or episodic rather than a globally reducing atmosphere.
Add pH and NH3 control or a competing lactonitrile branch, and replace rxn_012 with a specific enrichment mechanism.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: NiS-catalyzed acetylene hydration to acetaldehyde is experimentally supported, but the alanine-producing sequence is low-yield and condition-sensitive in the literature. The pathway also lacks an explicit transport or concentration step moving hydrothermal acetaldehyde into a surface HCN and NH3 Strecker setting, and the final L-enrichment remains unsupported.
suggestions: Insert an explicit transport or concentration step for acetaldehyde moving from the NiS hydrothermal system to the surface Strecker setting.
Capture the low-yield, pH-dependent nature of the NiS plus Strecker sequence and replace rxn_012 with a defined enrichment step.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is connected, molecule IDs are consistent, and the deterministic balance check reports 0 UNBALANCED reactions. That said, rxn_001, rxn_002, rxn_004, rxn_005, rxn_007, rxn_008, and rxn_011 should be written with explicit stoichiometric coefficients. Literature alignment is strong: the design centers the two dominant alanine hubs, correctly treats abiotic alanine as DL or near-racemic, and honestly separates L-enrichment from alanine synthesis. The main shortcomings are that rxn_012 is only a placeholder with no chemically specified, experimentally supported L-enrichment mechanism; rxn_001 is experimentally real but currently low-yield; rxn_002 is a heavily lumped version of Fe-S and CO pyruvate chemistry; rxn_005 misrepresents the mixed Fe(II)/Fe(III) oxyhydroxide system; and P10 lacks justified inter-environment transfer. Overall, this is a good network for prebiotic alanine pool formation, but not a high-confidence network for the specific target L-alanine. If the target were alanine or DL-alanine, the score would be materially higher.
